en: I was his very own.
There is no end if I keep telling it.
Ah, orphan, my tales are as many as ants.
When I was a little girl,
My hair was not yet long enough to braid,
My sorrowful head, lost in thought,
Had not yet passed twelve.
While I lived with my father,
I put on airs, poor soul.
Let me tell of my wretched life.
As a token of his fond indulgence,
Saying, 'Their rump meat will be sweet,'
My poor father Esen Khan
Had a hundred foals slaughtered.
With beaded plumes and coral stones,
Their chief ruler mingled among them,
He stationed a hundred guards.
His sentries were beyond counting,
His marksmen were more numerous still.
There are many things to tell.
Among the year's twelve months,
There is a month called Chagaan.
When that Chagaan came,
To the fortress in Beijing,
When the Chinese thronged and filled it,
Of the massed Chinese and Manchus
He would hear the people's words.
Before the khan of China,
I would go out for pleasure.
Then my ill-fated father Esen Khan,
Whenever I, poor thing, went out,
Had little bells made of gold
Fastened to my earlobes.
Saying, 'Allah's sun will strike her face,'
Draw a smile,
Of precious stones and rubies,
A necklace was made
And fastened round my neck.
A parrot's tail,
Shimmering ninety different ways,
He had fixed to my skullcap.
Of the Torgout, Manchu and Chinese,
He made the dignitaries look upon me.
Saying, 'Her steps will raise dust,'
My poor father Esen Khan
Had carpets laid before me,
And flowers of red and varied colors
Planted all around me.
Saying, 'Let her enjoy the cool breeze,'
He dressed him in a loose silk robe,
Saying, 'Let her play her fill,'
He set me on a smoothly moving pacer.
My pampered ways, among the people,
Became known to all.
My beauty, in the Khakan's
Genealogical register, was recorded.
My land breathed the fragrance of paradise.
Bringing my elder brother trouble and quarrels,
Many giants of Beijing asked for me.
The Chinese people's broad, brightly colored dresses—
I was the one who refused to wear them.
Saying, 'An unbeliever of a dark faith,'
To the mighty khan of the Manchus
I was the one who refused to wed.
When I lived in Beijing,
I was the beauty among women,
Of my father, the great Khan Esen,
I was the only daughter born into this world.
When I speak, my words to Allah are lament.
If you ask of Esen Khan's sons,
He had thirty-four sons.
The best of the thirty-four,
The deftest of the spearmen,
In the learning and lore of sorcery,
The one who knew surpassingly well,
Was famed Borukoz.
The youngest of the thirty-four officials,
His wrath made blood flow,
News of him made souls depart.
They inscribed Chinese writing on my hem.
My thirty-four elder brothers and my hero father
Gave me the name Burulcha.
When I reached twelve,
My waist bent as softly as cotton.
'Esen Khan's cherished daughter
Is extraordinarily beautiful,' they said—
By Beijing's Kara-Chinese
It was inscribed in their sacred book.
At six, I was a playing child;
When I reached eight,
I was intoxicated with being pampered.
When I reached nine,
My heart grew troubled,
The Kara-Chinese and Manchu
People seemed hateful to me.
My father Esen Khan's golden throne,
A yellow tree planted in the ridge,
At the foot of that tower
Was the white palace where treasure was piled.
No person ventured to its bank,
No mortal went there visiting,
No one had heard of it;
Anyone who saw it marveled.
A great palace in blue haze,
Its pillars iron, its foundations copper,
Within Tüp lay Chaar-Tal,
Its delights carved at great cost,
With openings cut in forty-one places,
With gemstones and rubies
He had it made bright.
On its cornice the unbelievers
Had written an inscription in Chinese:
“The palace of darling Burulcha”—
That was the name they gave the palace.
Inside that palace
No mortal came and went.
Among the black Chinese and Manchus
Not one of the people knew it.
The reason they did not know:
My father Esen Khan,
Calling me the fairest of women,
Had had thirty-four sons, all officials,
Then called me his daughter after them.
He listened to my words beyond measure,
And pampered me,
Having sixty mules and forty pigs
Slaughtered at the treasury's expense,
Saying someone might harm his daughter,
He levied a tax upon Beijing,
And summoned six thousand champions, magicians,
And spell-workers.
At the entrance of that palace
He displayed their arts through cunning,
Having dragons, boars, and beasts of prey
Set to guard the road.
At the entrance of that palace
Its tigers had bred fifteen times;
No person came along that way.
Its dragons numbered sixty;
Beyond them
It had learned human speech—
The red-naveled Chinese—
See their ways, like this:
There was an elephant with a sword-like nose.
In that palace's hollow,
Thirty noblewomen and thirty girls
While they were playing,
Into that palace
No person came and went.
Such was the khan's command:
If a man happened to appear,
Not a spoonful of his blood remained.
Fierce Hip Wing,
To his wife or daughter,
If another soul came visiting,
His custom was to kill him.
The teeming Chinese—
My doubled, trailing fringes,
The unbelievers of another faith
Made it their business to guard their wives,
A custom from ages past.
In that locked palace fortress,
Pampered as I grew, unfortunate me,
When I reached twelve years of age,
A playful little girl myself,
My age had not yet passed twelve.
Drawn toward the north,
A curtain patterned with gold,
Thirty-four quilts and ten pillows
Made my bed, unfortunate me.
Six noblewomen and eight girls
While we were enjoying ourselves,
Upon that bed,
On Friday's Night of Power,
When I lay down at leisure,
It was the Night of Power as I lay there;
The holy seer himself entered my dream.
Alake, who had gone to the other world—
It was when he came to tell of his ways.
“Ah, ah, ah, my child Burulcha,
Wake with a start from your sleep,
Turn onto your right side.
What you see today is gone tomorrow;
Such is this shitty world.
Saying that no man would now travel,
You were a son of light,
She was the daughter of Light;
Know well what I tell you:
Tomorrow, on the Day of Judgment,
My child, marry him as his bride.
The six kinds of stars in heaven are your guides.
‘May God make him yours forever,
The companion you are to marry—
His deeds will soothe your soul,
His ways will make your soul rejoice.
Indeed, this husband you shall marry is a saint;
His heroism is known to the people.
This is the place that will welcome you;
This is the man who will find your money.
Your treasure gathered in this world,
Your faith if you die,
Your guiding star in the sky,
Your companion if you marry.
He is the hero who will brighten your face;
He is the man who will care for you without sorrow.
Almambet, son of Azyz Khan—
To the young son of Oyrong,
Join yourself to him, my child.”
The saint who entered my dream
Said exactly this.
When the old man had spoken so,
I turned onto my right side.
Girded with a silver belt,
His sun-like face was radiant;
Girded with a golden belt,
His moon-like face was radiant.
He never drew back from reaching forward,
And never lost his stern expression.
With brown eyes free of any film,
With a white face free of freckles,
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Both a champion and a lion,
Almighty God in his power
Had given him to me there in my dream.
Telling us to enjoy ourselves,
To lie at play, two lovers,
He gave Almambet into my hands,
And the dervish vanished.
I was filled with delight;
With noble Almam the lion
I lay together in an embrace.
As I slept in my dream that day,
Of joyful games and pleasure
I had my fill.
Joining when I was tiny as a louse,
Uniting when I was small as a thumb,
Thinking him my cherished husband,
I lay playing until dawn.
Of this damned world
I had enjoyed the delights.
I saw this false world;
I came to know its passing nature.
That day, my wretched soul
Burned and blazed in anguish.
Yesterday, when clear dawn broke,
When light fell upon the earth,
When the Taraza stars set,
When clear dawn rose,
Waking with a start from sleep,
Turning onto my right side,
I leaped up.
What God has done—
There is no choice but to bear it.
When I leaped up,
It had been a sleeping dream;
There was no such mortal in my arms.
